title: parse user
statement:
Python Engineer · Typing and static analysis

Build parse_user

Validate an untrusted dict into a UserRecord.

- "id" must be present and int-convertible (a bool is NOT acceptable) -> else ValueError

- "name" must be a non-empty string after stripping -> else ValueError

- "email" must be a string containing "@" -> else ValueError

- Extra keys are dropped.

- The returned "name" is stripped.

- Error messages must name the offending field, e.g. "invalid email".

This is the hand-rolled version of what pydantic does for you in module 15 —

do it once by hand so you know what the library is buying you.

Work through this step

  1. Read the contract and identify its boundary cases.
  2. Run the demonstration to explore the concept.
  3. Edit the module file; focus on this step’s function or class.
  4. Run required checks, then explain one design decision in Notes.
Hint

Start with the smallest example in the contract. Read the named failing test; separate the normal behavior from validation and edge cases. Related helpers share this module workspace.

Module concepts & examples

07 — Typing and static analysis

Type hints are not enforced at runtime. They exist for mypy, your editor, and the

next person reading the code. On a codebase of any size they pay for themselves within a

week.

From here on, run make typecheck as often as make test.

In plain English

Python doesn't care what type things are. You can pass a string where the author obviously

meant a number, and Python will cheerfully try it and blow up somewhere else entirely, ten

minutes later, in a completely different file.

Type hints are notes you write in the code — def add(a: int, b: int) -> int — saying

what you actually meant. Python itself still ignores them completely at runtime. But a tool

called mypy reads them and tells you, before you ever run the program, "line 84 passes a

string here, and that's going to break."

It's a spell-checker for your code's plumbing. On a small script it's mild convenience. On a

big codebase it's the difference between refactoring confidently and refactoring by prayer.

The most valuable idea in here is Protocol: instead of saying "I need a Postgres

database", you say "I need something that has a save method and a get method". Anything

with the right shape fits — including a simple fake you write for your tests. That one idea

reappears in modules 14, 15, and every project.

Watch out for: hints are checked by mypy, not by Python. If you need actual runtime

enforcement on untrusted data, that's pydantic (module 15) — a different tool for a

different job.

1. Modern syntax (3.10+/3.12+)

def f(a: int, b: str | None = None) -> list[dict[str, int]]: ...

- Builtin generics: list[int], dict[str, int], tuple[int, ...], set[str].

typing.List etc. are deprecated.

- X | None instead of Optional[X]; A | B instead of Union[A, B].

- from __future__ import annotations makes all annotations lazy strings — avoids most

forward-reference and circular-import pain.

- Prefer abstract parameter types and concrete return types:

def f(items: Iterable[int]) -> list[int] — accept anything, promise something specific.

2. Generics

3.12 syntax (clean, no TypeVar import):

def first[T](items: Sequence[T]) -> T: ...

class Stack[T]:
    def push(self, item: T) -> None: ...
    def pop(self) -> T: ...

Pre-3.12 / library-compatible syntax:

T = TypeVar("T")
class Stack(Generic[T]): ...

Bounded and constrained:

NumT = TypeVar("NumT", bound=float)          # anything float-compatible
StrOrBytes = TypeVar("StrOrBytes", str, bytes)   # exactly one of these

Variance in one line: a list[Dog] is *not* a list[Animal] (you could append a Cat),

but a Sequence[Dog] *is* a Sequence[Animal] (read-only). This is why your parameters

should be Sequence/Iterable/Mapping, not list/dict.

3. Protocol — structural typing

Nominal typing asks "does it inherit from X?". Structural asks "does it have the right

shape?". Protocols give you Go-style interfaces with zero coupling:

class SupportsClose(Protocol):
    def close(self) -> None: ...

def cleanup(items: Iterable[SupportsClose]) -> None:
    for item in items:
        item.close()

Any object with close() satisfies this — no registration, no base class, and it works on

third-party types you don't control. Add @runtime_checkable for isinstance support

(it only checks *method names*, not signatures).

This is the backbone of dependency inversion in Python (module 14).

4. The vocabulary you'll actually use

FeatureUse
TypedDictdict with a fixed key schema — JSON payloads, config
NamedTupletyped immutable record
Literal["a", "b"]an enum-ish set of allowed values
Finalthis name is never reassigned
ClassVar[T]class attribute, not an instance field
Annotated[int, Ge(0)]attach metadata (FastAPI/pydantic build on this)
TypeAlias / type X = ...name a complex type (3.12: type Json = ...)
Selfmethods returning their own type — fluent APIs, __enter__
Never / NoReturnfunctions that always raise or never return
Anythe escape hatch; every Any is a hole in your type coverage
cast(T, x)"trust me" — no runtime effect
TYPE_CHECKINGimport only for type checking, avoids circular imports
ParamSpec + Concatenatedecorators that preserve the wrapped signature
TypeGuard / TypeIsnarrowing functions (def is_str_list(v) -> TypeIs[list[str]])
overloaddifferent return types for different argument shapes

5. Decorators that don't destroy types

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")

def timed(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        ...
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

Without ParamSpec the decorated function collapses to (*args: Any) -> Any and you lose

checking at every call site.

6. mypy in practice

mypy .                       # uses [tool.mypy] in pyproject.toml
mypy --strict path/          # the setting you actually want on new code

Useful settings: disallow_untyped_defs, warn_return_any, no_implicit_optional,

warn_unused_ignores, strict_equality. Silence a specific line with

# type: ignore[error-code] — always with the code, never bare.

Adopting types in an existing codebase: enable --strict per-module via

[[tool.mypy.overrides]], starting with new files and the core domain model.

Alternatives: pyright/Pylance (faster, better inference, what VS Code uses),

ty and pyrefly (newer Rust-based checkers). mypy is still the reference.

7. Runtime validation is a *different* problem

Type hints don't validate anything at runtime. For untrusted input (HTTP bodies, config

files) use pydantic, which reads the same annotations and enforces them — module 15

builds a FastAPI service on exactly that.

Exercises

exercises_07.py, then pytest 07_typing and make typecheck — the tests check

behaviour, mypy checks the annotations. Both must pass.

Further reading

- typing docs (optional reading: https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html)

- mypy cheat sheet (optional reading: https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/cheat_sheet_py3.html)

- PEP 544 — Protocols (optional reading: https://peps.python.org/pep-0544/)

Required check source
import pytest

from courselib import impl

m = impl("07")


class TestStack:
    def test_push_returns_self_for_chaining(self):
        s = m.Stack()
        assert s.push(1) is s
        assert len(m.Stack().push(1).push(2)) == 2

    def test_lifo(self):
        s = m.Stack()
        s.push(1).push(2)
        assert s.pop() == 2
        assert s.pop() == 1

    def test_peek_does_not_remove(self):
        s = m.Stack().push(1)
        assert s.peek() == 1
        assert len(s) == 1

    def test_pop_empty_raises(self):
        with pytest.raises(IndexError, match="empty"):
            m.Stack().pop()

    def test_peek_empty_raises(self):
        with pytest.raises(IndexError):
            m.Stack().peek()

    def test_truthiness(self):
        assert not m.Stack()
        assert m.Stack().push(1)

    def test_iterates_top_first(self):
        s = m.Stack()
        s.push(1).push(2).push(3)
        assert list(s) == [3, 2, 1]

    def test_clear(self):
        s = m.Stack().push(1)
        s.clear()
        assert len(s) == 0

    def test_repr(self):
        s = m.Stack()
        s.push(1).push(2)
        assert repr(s) == "Stack([1, 2])"

    def test_subscripting_the_class_works(self):
        assert m.Stack[int]().push(1).pop() == 1

    def test_instances_are_independent(self):
        a, b = m.Stack(), m.Stack()
        a.push(1)
        assert len(b) == 0


class TestCloseAll:
    def test_closes_everything(self):
        closed = []

        class Thing:
            def __init__(self, name):
                self.name = name

            def close(self):
                closed.append(self.name)

        assert m.close_all([Thing("a"), Thing("b")]) == []
        assert closed == ["a", "b"]

    def test_keeps_going_after_a_failure(self):
        closed = []

        class Bad:
            def close(self):
                raise OSError("cannot close")

        class Good:
            def close(self):
                closed.append("good")

        errors = m.close_all([Bad(), Good(), Bad()])
        assert closed == ["good"]
        assert len(errors) == 2
        assert all(isinstance(e, OSError) for e in errors)

    def test_empty_input(self):
        assert m.close_all([]) == []

    def test_protocol_is_runtime_checkable(self):
        class Thing:
            def close(self):
                pass

        assert isinstance(Thing(), m.SupportsClose)
        assert not isinstance(object(), m.SupportsClose)


class TestParseUser:
    def test_valid(self):
        assert m.parse_user({"id": 1, "name": "ada", "email": "a@b.c"}) == {
            "id": 1,
            "name": "ada",
            "email": "a@b.c",
        }

    def test_coerces_string_id(self):
        assert m.parse_user({"id": "42", "name": "n", "email": "a@b"})["id"] == 42

    def test_strips_name(self):
        assert m.parse_user({"id": 1, "name": "  ada  ", "email": "a@b"})["name"] == "ada"

    def test_drops_extra_keys(self):
        got = m.parse_user({"id": 1, "name": "n", "email": "a@b", "admin": True})
        assert set(got) == {"id", "name", "email"}

    @pytest.mark.parametrize(
        ("raw", "field"),
        [
            ({"name": "n", "email": "a@b"}, "id"),
            ({"id": "abc", "name": "n", "email": "a@b"}, "id"),
            ({"id": True, "name": "n", "email": "a@b"}, "id"),
            ({"id": 1, "email": "a@b"}, "name"),
            ({"id": 1, "name": "   ", "email": "a@b"}, "name"),
            ({"id": 1, "name": 5, "email": "a@b"}, "name"),
            ({"id": 1, "name": "n"}, "email"),
            ({"id": 1, "name": "n", "email": "nope"}, "email"),
            ({"id": 1, "name": "n", "email": None}, "email"),
        ],
    )
    def test_rejects_bad_input(self, raw, field):
        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match=field):
            m.parse_user(raw)

    def test_result_is_a_plain_dict(self):
        assert type(m.parse_user({"id": 1, "name": "n", "email": "a@b"})) is dict


class TestCounted:
    def test_counts(self):
        @m.counted
        def f(n):
            return n

        assert f.calls == 0
        f(1)
        f(2)
        assert f.calls == 2

    def test_reset(self):
        @m.counted
        def f():
            pass

        f()
        f.reset()
        assert f.calls == 0

    def test_return_value_passes_through(self):
        @m.counted
        def add(a, b=0):
            return a + b

        assert add(1, b=2) == 3

    def test_exceptions_propagate_and_still_count(self):
        @m.counted
        def boom():
            raise ValueError

        with pytest.raises(ValueError):
            boom()
        assert boom.calls == 1

    def test_preserves_metadata(self):
        @m.counted
        def documented():
            """Docs."""

        assert documented.__name__ == "documented"
        assert documented.__doc__ == "Docs."

    def test_separate_counters_per_function(self):
        @m.counted
        def a():
            pass

        @m.counted
        def b():
            pass

        a()
        assert b.calls == 0


class TestResult:
    def test_ok_and_err_construction(self):
        assert m.Ok(1).value == 1
        assert m.Err("bad").error == "bad"

    def test_is_ok(self):
        assert m.is_ok(m.Ok(1))
        assert not m.is_ok(m.Err("bad"))

    def test_unwrap_or(self):
        assert m.unwrap_or(m.Ok(5), 0) == 5
        assert m.unwrap_or(m.Err("bad"), 0) == 0

    def test_unwrap_or_with_falsy_value(self):
        assert m.unwrap_or(m.Ok(0), 99) == 0
        assert m.unwrap_or(m.Ok(None), 99) is None

    def test_map_ok(self):
        assert m.map_ok(m.Ok(2), lambda n: n * 3) == m.Ok(6)

    def test_map_passes_err_through(self):
        err = m.Err("bad")
        assert m.map_ok(err, lambda n: n * 3) is err

    def test_map_catches_exceptions(self):
        result = m.map_ok(m.Ok(0), lambda n: 1 / n)
        assert not m.is_ok(result)
        assert isinstance(result.error, ZeroDivisionError)

    def test_chaining(self):
        result = m.map_ok(m.map_ok(m.Ok(2), lambda n: n + 1), str)
        assert m.unwrap_or(result, "") == "3"

    def test_frozen_and_equal_by_value(self):
        assert m.Ok(1) == m.Ok(1)
        with pytest.raises(Exception):
            m.Ok(1).value = 2

"""Module 07 exercises.  pytest 07_typing  AND  make typecheck

This module is graded twice: the tests check runtime behaviour, mypy checks your
annotations. Fully annotate everything you write here — `disallow_untyped_defs` is on
for this file in pyproject.toml.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from typing import Any, ParamSpec, Protocol, TypedDict, TypeVar

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")


class Stack[T]:
    """A generic LIFO stack, using the 3.12 type-parameter syntax.

    - `push(item) -> Self` so calls chain: `Stack[int]().push(1).push(2)`.
    - `pop() -> T` raises IndexError("pop from empty stack") when empty.
    - `peek() -> T` returns the top without removing it; same error when empty.
    - `__len__`, `__bool__` (free via `__len__`), `__iter__` top-to-bottom,
      `__repr__` == "Stack([1, 2])" (bottom-to-top, like the underlying list).
    - `.clear()` empties it.

    mypy must be able to prove that `Stack[int]().pop()` is an `int`.
    """

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError


class SupportsClose(Protocol):
    """Structural interface: anything with a no-argument `close()` satisfies it.

    Leave the body as `...` — a Protocol declares shape, it doesn't implement it.
    Mark it `@runtime_checkable` so the tests can use `isinstance`.
    """

    def close(self) -> None: ...


def close_all(items: Iterable[SupportsClose]) -> list[BaseException]:
    """Close every item, and keep going even if some raise.

    Returns the list of exceptions raised, in order. An empty list means all clean.
    Every item must get its `close()` called, regardless of earlier failures — that's
    the whole point of a cleanup routine.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


class UserRecord(TypedDict):
    """The shape of a validated user."""

    id: int
    name: str
    email: str


def parse_user(raw: dict[str, Any]) -> UserRecord:
    """Validate an untrusted dict into a UserRecord.

    - "id" must be present and int-convertible (a bool is NOT acceptable) -> else ValueError
    - "name" must be a non-empty string after stripping                  -> else ValueError
    - "email" must be a string containing "@"                            -> else ValueError
    - Extra keys are dropped.
    - The returned "name" is stripped.
    - Error messages must name the offending field, e.g. "invalid email".

    This is the hand-rolled version of what pydantic does for you in module 15 —
    do it once by hand so you know what the library is buying you.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


def counted(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    """A decorator that counts calls WITHOUT destroying the wrapped signature.

    - `func.calls` starts at 0 and increments on every call.
    - `func.reset()` sets it back to 0.
    - Uses `ParamSpec` so mypy still checks arguments at every call site
      (a plain `Callable[..., Any]` would silently disable that).
    - Preserves metadata with `functools.wraps`.
    - Exceptions still propagate — and still count as a call.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError


class Result[T, E]:
    """A tiny Rust-style Result: either a value or an error, never both.

    Build it as TWO generic dataclasses plus a type alias:

        @dataclass(frozen=True)
        class Ok[T]: value: T
        @dataclass(frozen=True)
        class Err[E]: error: E
        type Result[T, E] = Ok[T] | Err[E]

    Then implement the free functions below. Replace this placeholder class entirely —
    the tests import `Ok`, `Err`, `is_ok`, `unwrap_or` and `map_ok` by name.
    """


def is_ok(result: Any) -> bool:
    """True for an Ok, False for an Err. Use `isinstance` — or `match`, which is nicer."""
    raise NotImplementedError


def unwrap_or(result: Any, default: Any) -> Any:
    """The value for Ok, `default` for Err."""
    raise NotImplementedError


def map_ok(result: Any, func: Callable[[Any], Any]) -> Any:
    """Apply `func` to an Ok's value, returning a new Ok. Pass an Err through untouched.

    If `func` raises, return `Err(exception)` — mapping must never blow up the pipeline.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError
